step1_summary: Chief complaint: Intensely itchy, red, sore skin rash disturbing sleep and work.

Symptom details: • Onset 4 days ago. • Location – chest, hands, inner elbows (no face, no legs). • Very pruritic; skin feels dry and ‘cracked.’ • No bleeding, pus, or discharge. • No fever, systemic symptoms, cough, dyspnea, urinary or bowel changes. • OTC steroid cream and OTC antihistamines tried without relief; showers give transient relief.
Past medical history: Atopic eczema in the past (limited to arms); childhood/previous asthma now resolved.
Medications / allergies: No regular meds. Recently used OTC topical steroid and OTC antihistamines. No known drug or other allergies.

Family / social history: 31-year-old male* living with flat-mates; project manager at a pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; drinks a few beers per week; enjoys hiking. (*sex inferred from transcript: doctor addresses ‘sir’).
Vital signs / exam: None documented; video exam implied but no specific descriptors other than ‘rash appears familiar, dry, cracked, erythematous.’

V: Urticaria secondary to physical/pressure stimulus: acute onset, widespread pruritus.
I: Scabies infestation: intensely pruritic rash involving hands and flexural areas; sleep disturbance.
Superficial fungal infection (tinea corporis/versicolor): erythematous pruritic patches.
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): chronic eczematous or psoriasiform lesions, but less likely with sudden 4-day onset.
D: Dermatitis herpetiformis (gluten-sensitive enteropathy): pruritic vesicles; elbows commonly involved.
I2: Drug-induced exanthematous eruption: possible but patient denies new medications.
C: Ichthyosis vulgaris flare: congenital dry, itchy skin, may overlap with atopy.
A: Atopic dermatitis flare: past history, pruritus, flexural distribution.
Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., new detergent, shower gel, clothing dye): acute onset, erythema, pruritus.
T: Irritant dermatitis from friction or environmental exposure (e.g., hiking gear, sweating).
E: Pruritus of cholestasis or renal failure: generalized itch, but no systemic clues.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Previous eczema history, classic pruritus, flexural involvement, dry cracked skin, no systemic illness, common exacerbations.
Acute onset after possible exposure to new detergent/soap/clothing; distribution includes chest & hands; itch prominent; prior creams ineffective.
Intense generalized pruritus (often worse at night), hand involvement, living with flat-mates (potential spread). Lack of response to steroids/antihistamines raises suspicion.
Pruritic erythematous lesions can appear suddenly, but patient describes dry/cracked skin rather than transient wheals.
Could cause erythematous itchy patches but distribution and rapid spread less typical; no ring-like lesions described.

supporting_evidence: Pruritus is intense and chronic feature of eczema.
opposing_evidence: New wider distribution (chest, hands) than previous flare.
Lack of improvement with OTC steroid after one day (though brief trial).

supporting_evidence: Hands and chest commonly exposed to soaps/detergents/clothes.
Patient unsure if any product change (possible unrecognized exposure).
opposing_evidence: No clear history of new product or exposure.

supporting_evidence: Lives with multiple flat-mates – transmission risk.
opposing_evidence: No burrows, nodules, or lesions on finger webs reported.
Abrupt 4-day onset (scabies often evolves over weeks).
No itching reported in contacts (though not asked).
Skin described as dry/cracked rather than transient raised wheals.
Persistence over multiple days without waxing/waning.
No annular scaling borders; widespread simultaneous onset uncommon.
